Create a table, store user preferences, conversation history, task summaries, and attach vector search. When needed, search and splice results into the prompt, and the model "remembers". This version works and does solve some problems. But it quickly hits several issues: 1. Not everything stored should have long-term influence on the future. The user casually says "ignore testing for now" today — is that a current time crunch, or a long-term preference? If such items lack source, scope, and time, once saved as "memory", they cannot be easily disambiguated later. 2. What is retrieved may not fit the current task. When the user asks "help me change the cache strategy", the semantically closest match might be a previous conversation about Redis. But what ultimately changes the design choice could be a record of a failed load test during a big sale three months ago. Similarity does not equal suitability. 3. Memory expires. Preferences change, projects change, team rules change, and model capabilities change. A system that cannot forget will eventually be dragged down by its own stale experience. Later I came to see Agent Memory as a control plane layer in the Harness. Understanding it only as a storage layer misses the hardest part. Storage only answers "where things go". Memory must answer at least this list: what is worth writing, in whose identity it is written, over what scope it is valid, when to lower its weight, which source to trust when it conflicts with old memories, how to roll back if it is polluted or written incorrectly, and whether users can view, modify, and delete.
